title: Three quarters of dentists have or aspire to have a portfolio career
html:
Four in 10 dentists (41%) said they already have a portfolio career in a new survey, while a further third (33%) would like to build one.

Portfolio careers are becoming more popular in dentistry, with many dentists splitting their time between NHS, private care, teaching and other roles. In Wesleyan Financial Services’ Navigating the Future of NHS Dentistry whitepaper, 18% of surveyed dentists were actively planning to build a portfolio career.

Just 12% said they planned to stay in the NHS until retirement, with 21% planning a gradual shift towards private care. More than one in five (22%) said they planned to leave the dental profession entirely within the next five years.

What makes a portfolio career appealing?

According to the survey respondents, the main appeal of a portfolio career is work-life balance (56%), professional growth (45%), and variety (40%). However, workload (48%) and admin (33%) were cited as significant downsides.

While 41% of dentists said that retaining some NHS work was very important to them, 79% said the current contract is unfit or needs major reform.

Lauren Harrhy, principal dentist at Sparkle Dental Centre, said: ‘None of us really want to give up the NHS entirely because we feel duty bound to take care of patients from all walks of life. But it comes to a point when we find that the restrictions around the NHS contract mean that we can’t always care for people in the manner that we want to.’

Funding was the largest grievance, with 73% saying the contract is inadequately funded for good patient care and 81% believing NHS dentists are not fairly compensated.

Nigel Jones, Practice Plan’s strategy director, highlighted the lack of new investment into NHS dentistry. He said: ‘It all comes back to the fact that the pot of money for NHS dentistry is the same, if not shrinking.’

Is there hope for the future of NHS dentistry?

The 2026 changes to the contract have not reassured the profession: 47% called them minor tweaks and 13% said they made matters worse. Seven in 10 (71%) said the government’s direction with reform is still unclear.

The surveyed dentists strongly rejected the UDA model. Two thirds (66%) said it is no longer fit for purpose, and only 5% thought the current UDA rate is appropriate. Many believed activity-based payment for complex cases would be a better replacement.

Eddie Crouch, chair of the British Dental Association (BDA), agreed that the government’s future plans for dentistry were difficult to discern. He asked: ‘Are we going to get a targeted system? Is it going to be a core system? Or are we going to be left in limbo?’

With dentists leaving the NHS at a rapid rate, he suggested that increased competition might force private practices to take a hit to their income.

Iain Stevenson, head of dental at Wesleyan, said it had shared the research in the report to ‘help drive the debate around how best to create a system that works for everyone’. He continued: ‘The UK has a shortage of dentists, but no lack of patients, and it’s clear that many clinicians are as frustrated by this state of affairs as their patients.

‘Dentists want real reform so they can deliver the kind of high-quality service that they were trained to do, but they lack confidence that adequate change can be achieved in short order. This scepticism is driving widespread disillusionment, which threatens to drive more dentists away from the NHS, further undermining the service and accelerating its decline.’
